full_text:

Investing.com-- Asian stocks were mixed in choppy trade on Tuesday, as a record Nasdaq close overnight offered some support, while elevated U.S. Treasury yields and oil prices limited risk appetite.
Some Asian equities followed a strong Wall Street session. The Nasdaq rose 1.1% to a record close on Monday, while the S&P 500 gained 0.7% and the Dow rose 0.2%.

The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.349% overnight, its highest since 2002, while the 30-year yield reached 5.703%.
Elevated Treasury yields weigh on equities by raising borrowing costs and making bonds more attractive relative to riskier assets, particularly in high-growth technology shares.
RBI decision due this week; Brent remains above $100
Elsewhere, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.6%, while Singapore’s Straits Times Index edged down 0.2%.
Futures tied to India’s Nifty 50 ticked down 0.1%.
Investors were looking ahead to the Reserve Bank of India’s policy decision on Wednesday, with markets expecting a 25-basis-point rate hike.
Markets also awaited the minutes of the Fed’s September meeting, due on Wednesday, for clues on policymakers’ views about inflation and the timing of further rate increases.
Oil prices remained a key risk. Brent crude was around $100 a barrel after falling 1.9% on Monday as Middle East exports increased and the Group of Seven pledged to boost supplies. Investors remained alert to renewed disruptions from the U.S.-Iran conflict.

title: Gold holds near $4,140 as dollar, yields offset lower Fed hike expectations
full_text:
Wall Street ends within sight of record close as traders brush off bond rout
Investing.com -- Gold prices were little changed on Tuesday after recovering from their biggest weekly decline since June, as a stronger U.S. dollar and elevated Treasury yields offset support from fading expectations for another Federal Reserve rate hike.
At 20:44 ET (00:44 GMT), XAU/USD fell 0.1% to $4,138.09 an ounce, while Gold Futures rose 0.2% to $4,165.15. XAG/USD fell 0.1% to $60.998, while XPT/USD declined 0.2% to $1,721.37. The U.S. Dollar Index was little changed at 102.17.
Stronger dollar, Treasury yields weigh on gold
Gold's recovery has come as investors assess growing fiscal pressure around the world and the implications for monetary policy.
In Europe, political uncertainty and fiscal concerns in France have supported demand for the dollar. Policy gridlock triggered a selloff in more vulnerable European government debt and pushed the euro to a 17 month low, lifting the greenback toward its strongest levels of the year.
A stronger dollar typically pressures gold by making the metal more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
French debt concerns have also added to the broader rise in global bond yields. Bank of France Governor Emmanuel Moulin warned that France could become increasingly constrained by high interest costs if it fails to improve its public finances, as French bond yields continued to rise.
U.S. Treasuries also came under fresh pressure Monday, with longer dated yields reaching new multi decade highs as the bond market extended a months long decline. Higher yields increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which does not generate interest income.
A U.S. Institute for Supply Management report showed cost pressures in the services sector rose last month at their fastest pace in more than four years. Persistent price pressures have kept the possibility of further Fed tightening alive, despite a weaker labor market.
Interest rate swaps were showing an almost 23% probability of an October Fed hike, while markets continued to price a full quarter point increase by the December meeting.
Weaker jobs data lowers near term rate hike bets
Gold has fallen more than 6% in September as energy driven inflation concerns, expectations for higher U.S. rates and a stronger dollar weighed on the metal.
However, expectations for an immediate Fed increase have eased sharply since last week's weaker than expected U.S. payrolls report. Fed officials have also been pushing back against expectations of an imminent hike.
That shift has provided some support for gold, even as rising bond yields remain a constraint.
The minutes of the Fed's September meeting, when policymakers raised interest rates for the first time in three years, are due midweek and could provide further guidance on the policy outlook.
ANZ analysts said gold has recovered from last week's sharp decline as investors reassess rising fiscal pressures globally.
They also pointed to lower expectations for rate hikes following the weaker payrolls data, with markets now assigning roughly a 20% chance of an October hike, down from around 70% a week earlier.

full_text:

Trump’s exemption comes as U.S. diesel prices surged to record highs due to supply disruptions stemming from the Middle East and interruptions in refining due to the Russia-Ukraine war.

title: Australian consumer sentiment falls more than expected as rate, fuel costs bite
full_text:

Investing.com -- Australian consumer confidence deteriorated sharply, with households increasingly concerned about their finances, the economic outlook and jobs as cost-of-living pressures intensified, data from Westpac showed on Tuesday.
The Westpac-Melbourne Institute Consumer Sentiment Index fell 4.7% to 80.4 from 84.4 in September, missing a forecast 1.2% decline that would have put the index at about 83.4. The 80.4 reading was also among the weakest recorded since the survey began in the early 1970s.
Westpac said the latest Reserve Bank of Australia rate increase to 4.6%, the highest level since 2011, appears to have sharply rattled consumers.
Sentiment among the 60% of respondents surveyed before the rate decision was 86.9, but plunged to 67.2 among those surveyed after the announcement.
The nearly 20% difference between the pre- and post-RBA samples was the largest since Westpac began tracking daily survey responses in 2019, the bank said.
Fuel prices have also become a major drag, with average weekly pump prices rising above A$2.30 a litre, nearly 25% higher than at the start of the year. Meanwhile, the standard variable mortgage rate is expected to move above 9%, according to Westpac.
Westpac said pessimists outnumbered optimists in 102 of 106 consumer groups tracked by the survey, while more than 80% of consumers expected mortgage rates to rise over the next year.
The report also showed growing unease about the jobs outlook, suggesting pressure on household finances is broadening beyond inflation and borrowing costs.

title: Anthropic tells Australia it’s open to laws requiring reporting of AI agent hacks
full_text:
Wall Street ends within sight of record close as traders brush off bond rout
By Byron Kaye
SYDNEY, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Anthropic does not believe its products have breached Australian government systems but would be open to Australian laws requiring AI companies to disclose data breaches, company executives told an Australian parliamentary inquiry on Tuesday.
Their statements come weeks after rival OpenAI disclosed one of its agents broke into the country’s main health portal and as the companies wait for approval for massive data centres planned in Sydney and regional Queensland.
Anthropic, creator of AI chatbot Claude, and ChatGPT maker OpenAI also want Australia to relax its copyright laws so they can use local content to train models.
Australia, which is readying AI-specific laws that will take effect next year, rebuked OpenAI in September after the US tech firm notified it of a breach of the Medicare portal some three months earlier.
Both firms are under scrutiny worldwide after incidents in which their AI agents have gone rogue to hack external systems, learning to bend rules, exploit loopholes and interact with external systems.
Anthropic Head of Safeguards David Orr told the parliamentary inquiry into AI that a "lengthy, deep investigation" since an OpenAI agent’s hack of Hugging Face, showed there had been no breaches of Australian government systems.
"We haven’t found anything like this, and we have looked," he said.
The company had "much less visibility on what has happened for our customers", Orr noted, since enterprise customers typically had stricter rules on data deletion.
Whether a company reported a breach of government data was most likely determined by the company’s internal policy, not the law, Orr said. Anthropic’s head of policy for Australia and New Zealand, David Masters, told the inquiry the company would be open to Australian laws requiring AI companies to disclose data breaches.
At the inquiry, Australian content creators pushed back against attempts by AI companies to relax copyright laws which currently require the mostly foreign-domiciled tech companies to negotiate licencing deals before using their material for model training.
"The copyright system is completely adequate to manage the business of AI," said Kate Gilchrist, the head of content and legal operations for national broadcaster the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.
Media reports have said the Australian government was considering an "opt out" clause for AI companies, effectively giving the AI companies access to content unless a rightsholder objects, but that "places the burden on rightsholders", said Gilchrist.
"We cannot scour the internet and ensure that we are opting out on all those sites. It simply does not work," she said.
The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is one of at least four Australian state and federal inquiries into the technology.
Representatives of OpenAI are scheduled to appear at the same inquiry later on Tuesday.

title: Exclusive-Accenture contractor removed from FBI following damaging data breach, sources say
full_text:
Wall Street ends within sight of record close as traders brush off bond rout
By Jana Winter and Raphael Satter
WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The Federal Bureau of Investigation removed an Accenture contractor on Monday over their role in a damaging data breach that exposed sensitive personal details of thousands of bureau employees, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The development comes as the FBI is still trying to ascertain the ramifications of the breach, which some former bureau officials have described as a major blow to the organization’s operational security.
In a statement to Reuters, a senior FBI official confirmed that an unidentified contractor had failed to properly update — or patch — the system they were responsible for.
"To date, our review has determined that the incident occurred as the result of a security failure of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the platform," FBI cyber chief Brett Leatherman said in the statement. "As such, the FBI has removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our workforce."
The FBI did not identify the platform or third-party organization, but the two sources familiar with the matter said the platform was Oracle’s PeopleSoft, a human resources platform that the hacking group ShinyHunters said it exploited to break into the FBI’s job site last month.
Oracle did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
The sources also said the third-party organization was Accenture. Reuters could not immediately identify the specific contractor or determine their current employment status.
In a statement, Accenture said it was "proud to support the mission of the FBI and will continue to do so." It did not answer questions about the contractor or their alleged failure to patch.
CRITICAL PATCHES
In June, Google raised the alarm over a ShinyHunters-linked hack-and-extort campaign aimed at organizations using PeopleSoft software. The same day, Oracle issued a security alert identifying a weakness in PeopleSoft and offering security fixes.
Both companies urged organizations running PeopleSoft to "apply all Critical Patch Updates, Critical Security Patch Updates and Security Alerts without delay."
Swift patching of vulnerable software is considered a key part of defending networks and devices against hackers, but the process can be laborious and difficult, particularly with enterprise software that serves large numbers of people.
Reuters has not been able to determine whether or when those responsible for securing the FBI’s job site followed those recommendations, but ShinyHunters credited a vulnerability in PeopleSoft for facilitating its intrusion.
The breach has triggered concern across the FBI and the wider intelligence community, exposing sensitive personal information, including granular descriptions of named employees’ counterintelligence jobs, street addresses of human intelligence operatives, and medical and psychiatric records of bureau workers.
Last week, a key ShinyHunters suspect was detained in Jordan, Reuters reported. Sources told Reuters the alleged hacker was cooperating, a development that may help the bureau limit — or at the very least understand — the scope of the damage.

By Jarrett Renshaw and Gram Slattery
GRAND ISLAND, Nebraska, Oct 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump pledged to expand access to tax-exempt diesel fuel while warning of a dark future if Democrats win the midterms during a rally on Monday night in Nebraska, a state where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices and inflation has weighed heavily on the rural economy.
His stop in the city of Grand Island was part of Trump’s 32-day sprint to the November 3 midterm elections, a campaign in which he is spending considerable time in conservative strongholds, helping defend Senate and House seats that until several months ago were considered safe for Republicans. Trump, as he has done in previous rallies, urged Republicans to “pretend” he is on the ballot, arguing that voters should view the midterms as a referendum on his administration and economic record.
"With your support, just 29 days from now, Nebraska is going to defeat the radical-left Dumb-o-crats once again," Trump said in the opening moments of his remarks.
His party is trying to persuade voters that investment, manufacturing and economic growth under Trump outweigh the pain of higher prices stemming from the unpopular US-Israeli war on Iran.
But Republicans enter the final weeks of the campaign facing a difficult national political environment. A Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday found Trump’s approval rating at 32%, matching the lowest reading of his political career, while registered voters preferred Democrats over Republicans 44% to 37% when asked which party they would support in the midterms. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% undecided.
Reuters polling and analysis have also found Republicans’ opponents competitive in a number of states Trump won by double digits in 2024, including Nebraska. Trump carried Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024, but public polling consistently shows a competitive contest between Republican Senator Pete Ricketts and independent Dan Osborn.
ORGANIZERS ADD HUNDREDS OF CHAIRS
During the rally, Trump flitted through various topics, from Iran to Venezuela to his legally and financially dubious pledge to give all adults $5,000 if the Republicans win the midterms.
He also suggested that Iran could "take out" a major US city like Los Angeles or San Diego, prompting swift backlash from California leaders and even some fellow Republicans.
He again attacked the media on multiple occasions and criticized former President Joe Biden, who has proven an enduring Trump foil, even as he has been out of office for almost two years. Throughout the speech, he painted a dark picture of America should the Democrats take control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
"They want to burn it down," Trump said of the Democratic Party. "Their whole life is talking about radicalization and stupidity."
The most significant policy news of the evening was the announcement of an executive order expanding access to red-dye diesel, which is exempt from some taxes but has generally been limited to off-road and agricultural uses.
Supporters were packed into the Heartland Events Center in Grand Island, many wearing Trump’s signature red shirts and others sporting University of Nebraska attire in the same shade. Organizers brought out hundreds of additional chairs to accommodate supporters in the rear of the arena, as the crowd filled available seating ahead of Trump’s remarks.
Trump has grown agitated at recent reporting of empty chairs and early departures at his signature rallies.
For many, the draw was the unusual sight of Trump in the Republican-heavy state of Nebraska. He has only visited the state about six times since 2016 and not once since 2022, public records show.
"I am not sure I will ever see him in person again and didn’t want to miss this. He doesn’t come here often," said Nancy Rhodes, a 54-year-old stay-at-home mother who drove an hour to see the president.
Rhodes said Trump’s decision to start a war with Iran has made things more expensive - and may hurt Trump’s party’s chances of retaining power - but said disarming Iran’s nuclear program was worth the cost.
Trump started his campaign swing last week with stops in Texas, Oklahoma, Alabama and Ohio, reflecting his goal of energizing voters in Republican-friendly states while making himself the central messenger for a party facing concerns about his political standing.
He told reporters on Monday that he plans to travel nearly every day until the November 3 midterms, including stops in Iowa and Michigan.

Samsung Electronics is the direct focal point of all three events simultaneously, making it the primary instrument through which investors in Korean semiconductors will feel Thursday's volatility.
Traders seeking a hedge or expression of the rebalancing flow should note that Goldman also flags mechanical buying pressure building in SK Hynix, SK Square, and equipment names including Isu Petasys, Wonik IPS, and Hanmi Semi as a counterpart to Samsung's expected mechanical selling.
On the earnings side, Goldman Sachs estimates Samsung's 3Q26 operating profit at W106 trillion, in line with street consensus of W105.5 trillion, according to Oh's note — though that figure represents a 5% cut from Goldman's prior estimate of W112 trillion.
The bank attributed the revision primarily to Korean won strength, with the average USD/KRW rate tracking around 1,418 versus Goldman's prior assumption of 1,460. Street consensus has itself declined from an August peak of roughly W114 trillion for the same reason.
Despite the estimate cut, Goldman maintained a constructive view on the operating fundamentals underpinning the result. "GIR believes W100tn+ OP is backed by solid DRAM/NAND fundamentals, with HBM growth the standout," Oh said.
Goldman expects Samsung's HBM bit shipments to grow close to 50% quarter-on-quarter in 3Q26, driven by the ramp of HBM4 shipments.
Conventional DRAM bit growth, by contrast, is described as "largely flattish given the limited level of inventory" because incremental capacity is being reallocated toward HBM production.
The ETF rebalancing layer adds a mechanical dimension that is largely independent of earnings quality. Seven semiconductor ETFs with combined assets under management of roughly W19 trillion (approximately $14 billion), according to Goldman, are scheduled to rebalance on October 8.
Local media and the street anticipate Samsung will face outflows due to a weighting cap in those vehicles, while SK Hynix and semiconductor equipment makers absorb the offsetting inflows.
Samsung's W15 trillion repurchase program was expected to be completed this week, eliminating a reliable source of daily buying support at a moment when selling pressure from multiple directions is elevated.
That selling pressure was already visible in the days leading into the event. Foreign investors were net sellers of Samsung for five consecutive days ahead of October 8, totaling net outflows of approximately $2.6 billion, according to Goldman's note.
The firm's own trading desk reported a sell-skewed flow pattern through September, with hedge funds more sell-biased than long-only accounts, and Oh noted the desk remained better sell-skewed on October 8 itself.
Looking beyond Thursday's event cluster, Goldman's watch list is straightforward. "Whether foreign inflows return back and company keeps the strong earnings momentum/guidance would be a key to watch," Oh wrote.

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon warned Tuesday that the release of Anthropic’s powerful Mythos AI system has exponentially escalated the financial sector’s cybersecurity vulnerabilities, cementing cyberattacks as the bank’s absolute biggest threat.
Speaking with Bloomberg TV’s Tom Mackenzie at the 14th annual JPMorgan Tech Summit in London, Dimon didn’t mince words about the mounting dangers of advanced AI agents.
"I published my chairman’s letter... I said cyber is our biggest risk," Dimon stated. "And they didn’t publish Mythos yet. I would say that went up tenfold after Mythos."
While Dimon acknowledged the immense potential for AI to "cure a lot of diseases," prevent traffic accidents, and revolutionize materials science, he stressed that the technology has also handed bad actors unprecedented leverage.
"AI created vulnerabilities that we didn’t know about, and we always worried about cyber before these things," Dimon explained. "The downside is obviously what you read about with the agents and Mythos and all these things that can cause trouble. And that’s a legitimate concern. It’s a real thing."
However, the Wall Street veteran noted he isn’t getting "hysterical" over whether AI poses an existential threat, adding, "What we’re doing is rolling up our sleeves and going to work to fix it." Part of that fix involves the newly formed Alliance for Critical Infrastructure, a 50-company coalition spanning six vital industries—including tech, finance, water, and transport—designed to fortify defenses against systemic threats.
Unchecked Debt and "Free" Policy
Beyond the digital frontier, Dimon sounded the alarm on ballooning sovereign debt, pointing to recent bond selloffs as a stark indicator of what happens when borrowing goes unchecked.
"It’s a warning to governments, okay: we can’t borrow endlessly and spend endlessly," Dimon cautioned. Noting that U.S. government debt has surged from 50% to 100% of GDP, he warned that "there will be a point where the market will ask for more and more," inevitably driving up corporate credit spreads and squeezing private markets.
Dimon also pushed back against the idea that boosting economic output requires massive fiscal expansion.
"This may be my next op-ed: Good policy is free," Dimon remarked. "Good policy in the United States and in Europe can drive growth 1% higher, and it does not cost money." He pointed to sensible improvements in permitting, education, deregulation, climate policy, and immigration as deflationary catalysts that could naturally drive down debt-to-GDP ratios.
The AI Infrastructure Boom
Addressing the massive capital expenditures projected for global AI infrastructure, Dimon pushed back on the politics of building massive data centers, half of which are currently slated for Texas and Virginia.
His advice to tech founders facing local resistance was blunt: go where you are welcomed.
"You build them where they’re wanted... people don’t want them there, you’re not going to win. You get lawsuits," Dimon said. "But there are a lot of states [that] would take it that have access to power. And of course, any big company has to be a good community citizen."
Despite a "little bit of a slowdown in September" for U.S. investment banking pipelines, Dimon remains largely optimistic about the broader tech ecosystem, noting that the London summit has grown from 20 attendees to thousands of global investors. "A lot of these companies, they’re real. They’re going to invent things that help mankind for hundreds of years," he said.

title: Goldman flags 2 key market risks if a climb in yields persists
full_text:
Wall Street marches higher, S&P 500 scales first record high since mid-August
Investing.com -- A sustained rise in interest rates could weigh on equity prices and revive concerns about U.S. fiscal sustainability, a Goldman Sachs economist argues, adding to a drag on economic growth that he currently sees as manageable.
Rates have risen sharply this year, and the latest jump in long-term yields has "tightened financial conditions noticeably,” economist Pierfrancesco Mei wrote.
Goldman’s baseline assumes one more Fed hike in December, followed by three cuts starting in the second half of 2027, with the 10-year Treasury yield easing from 5.3% to 4.4% by the end of 2027.
Under that scenario, the bank estimates higher rates will subtract about 0.2 percentage points from 2027 GDP growth, leaving the economy expanding close to its 2.3% potential. If current rates persist, the drag would rise to slightly over 0.5 percentage point.
Housing is the most exposed sector. With mortgage rates up more than 1 percentage point since February, over 90% of borrowers hold mortgages priced below market rates, giving them little incentive to move.
Mei expects higher rates to subtract about 2 percentage points from annualized residential investment growth in the fourth quarter and 1 point on average in 2027, with the drag roughly twice as large if rates stay at current levels.
Consumer spending growth should slow by about 0.2 percentage point in 2027, Mei noted, as higher rates curb credit-financed purchases of durable goods such as vehicles, partly offset by higher net interest income.
Business investment faces a 0.3-point drag as companies refinance debt at higher rates, with small businesses more exposed because about half their debt is variable-rate, the economist continued.
Until recently, Mei said, the drag from higher rates was roughly offset by higher equity prices, tighter credit spreads and a weaker dollar. Financial conditions are now tightening.
The first additional risk is to equities. Goldman’s strategists expect stocks to rise slightly over 10% by the end of 2027, but stable rates could limit that upside. “If equities were roughly flat through 2027 because of higher rates, the missing boost from wealth effects would lower consumer spending growth by just under 0.5pp,” Mei said.
The second is fiscal. Higher rates "have revived fiscal sustainability concerns," Mei wrote. The large primary deficit remains the main driver of rising debt, but persistently higher rates would raise interest costs and push the debt-to-GDP ratio up faster, increasing the odds that deficit reduction becomes necessary sooner, he added.

Indeed, imports are on track to have surged by between 25% and 30% annualized, whereas exports are likely to have fallen slightly.
